Rate of Reaction.q: How is rate of reaction calculated?
Rate of Reaction.a: Amount of product formed divided by time
d: Time divided by amount of product

Rate of Reaction.q: What does a steeper gradient on a rate graph indicate?
What does a flat line on a rate graph indicate?
Rate of Reaction.a: The reaction is complete - no more product being formed
d: The reaction has stopped due to low temperature
The rate is constant at zero

Factors Affecting Rate.q: According to collision theory, what is needed for a reaction to occur?
Factors Affecting Rate.a: Particles must collide with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy
d: Particles must be the same size
All particles in the mixture must react

Factors Affecting Rate.q: How does increasing temperature affect rate of reaction?
Factors Affecting Rate.a: Particles move faster - more frequent and more energetic collisions
d: Only the frequency of collisions increases
Temperature has no effect on rate

Factors Affecting Rate.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
Factors Affecting Rate.a: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
d: It increases the concentration of reactants
It is used up in the reaction

Factors Affecting Rate.q: Why does increasing surface area increase rate of reaction?
Factors Affecting Rate.a: More particles are exposed so collisions occur more frequently

Equilibrium.a: Forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates - concentrations remain constant
d: Products convert fully back to reactants

Equilibrium.q: According to Le Chatelier's principle if you increase temperature what happens?
Equilibrium.a: Equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction
d: Equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction

Equilibrium.q: Does adding a catalyst shift the position of equilibrium?
Equilibrium.a: No - it speeds up reaching equilibrium but does not change the position
d: Yes - it always shifts towards products
Yes - it shifts in the endothermic direction
